summary: This memo allocates code points for four new elliptic curve domain parameter sets over finite prime fields. They go into a registry established by the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) but used by other protocols as well.

eli5.summary: Secret-handshake math has a menu of curves to pick from. This adds four more choices to the menu.

questions: which ike group numbers are brainpool curves
why are twisted brainpool curves not registered
what is the ike group description registry
subtitle: Four Brainpool elliptic curves get code points in the IKE Group Description registry so other protocols can name them.

tldr.problem: The Brainpool curves of RFC 5639 had no entries in the IANA registry that maps complete elliptic curve parameter sets to short numbers, even though other protocols still use that registry.
tldr.mechanism: The memo copies the domain parameters of the 224, 256, 384 and 512-bit curves and has IANA assign values 27 to 30 for them, marked as not for use with RFC 2409.
tldr.outcome: The four curves can be referenced by number. The 160, 192 and 320-bit curves and all twisted curves were deliberately left out.

today: RFC 6932 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the registry entries for the four curves.

sections.title: Why Register Brainpool Curves
sections.content:
RFC 5639 defines elliptic curve domain parameters over several prime fields, each with a twisted variant. IANA keeps a registry created for RFC 2409 (the Internet Key Exchange) that maps complete domain parameter sets to easily referenced numbers.

RFC 2409 is deprecated, but other protocols, for example IEEE 802.11 and RFC 5931, still refer to the registry for its convenience. So this memo asks IANA to allocate new code points there for the Brainpool curves.
sections.eli5: There is a numbered list of math curves that many programs look at. This memo gets four new curves onto that list.

sections.title: Which Curves and Their Parameters
sections.content:
All curves use the equation y^2 = x^3 + ax + b (mod p). A parameter set gives the prime p, the curve parameters a and b, the generator coordinates x and y, the group order q, the co-factor h and the twist z. The memo prints these for each curve as hexadecimal values, and every curve has h = 1.

RFC 5639 covers seven prime field sizes, each in a random and a twisted form, fourteen curves in all. This memo adds only four: brainpoolP224r1, brainpoolP256r1, brainpoolP384r1 and brainpoolP512r1. The 160-bit curves give only 80 bits of strength, too small for current use. The 196-bit and 320-bit curves have no standard hash function, so the 224-bit and 384-bit curves are the sensible choice.

The twisted curves are not registered. They are isomorphic to the random curves, with a equal to -3 mod p. A point converts with (x',y') = (x*z^2, y*z^3), so an implementation can compute internally on the twisted curve while exchanging points on the random curve. Such implementations must take the full parameters from RFC 5639.
sections.eli5: Each curve is described by a handful of big numbers, like a recipe. The memo lists the recipes for four sizes and skips the ones that are too weak or awkward.

sections.title: The New Registry Entries
sections.content:
IANA assigned four values from the unassigned part of the Group Description component of the IKE registry. Each carries the note Not for RFC 2409.

The notes are an administrative prohibition, not a technical one. RFC 2409 is deprecated yet still widely used, and some in the IETF did not want to do anything that would prolong its use. The registry could not be updated without the notes, and leaving it alone would have hurt the other protocols that use it.
sections.eli5: The four new curves get numbers on the list, with a sticky note saying not to use them with one old protocol. The note is a request, not a technical block.

sections.title: Security Levels
sections.content:
The curves support security levels of 112 (224-bit), 128 (256-bit), 192 (384-bit) and 256 (512-bit). These levels assume the private key is a uniformly random number in the range 1 to q-1, where q is the order from the curve's domain parameters.

To get system security that matches the curve's level, an implementation has to choose key derivation functions, hash functions, pseudo-random functions and ciphers according to the recommendations in SP800-57.
sections.eli5: A strong lock is only as good as the key you cut for it. Each curve has a strength rating, and you have to pick the other parts to match.

sections.title: Test Data
sections.content: Appendix A provides a test vector for each of the four curves (brainpoolP224r1, brainpoolP256r1, brainpoolP384r1 and brainpoolP512r1). Implementers can use them to check that a curve implementation computes the expected values.
sections.eli5: The appendix has answer-key examples, so you can check that your own math comes out right.
